---
title: "How it works"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
```

peabiru's routing engine is written in Rust and runs inside the R session.
This page follows a request from the input files to the numbers, with the same diagrams as the
[Rust guide](../../rust/how-it-works.html). It describes what is computed
and in which order, not the data structures, which change as the engine is
optimised.

## One engine, three packages

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Architecture: an OpenStreetMap .pbf and GTFS .zip feeds go into peabiru-core, a Rust crate that builds the street network and transit layer in memory and computes every result; the R package, the Python package and the command line are front-ends over it."}
fig("architecture.svg")
```

The Rust crate `peabiru-core` does all the work. This R package checks the
arguments, converts points and results between R and Rust, and returns a
`data.frame`; the Python package (which returns pandas data frames) and the
`peabiru` command-line tool (CSV in, CSV out) do the same for their users.
There is no separate process to start and nothing is written to disk.

## Building the network

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Network build: the .pbf becomes a street network (edges with permissions, speeds and traffic stress, islands closed, index, park-and-ride, turn restrictions); GTFS feeds become patterns of trips; stops are linked to the streets; then walking transfers and egress distances are precomputed."}
fig("network-build.svg")
```

`build_network()` reads the `.pbf` and the GTFS feeds of a directory and keeps
the result in memory. The street network has one edge per direction of every
street segment, with the modes allowed on it, a car speed and, for cyclists, a
level of traffic stress; public transport is grouped into *patterns* (trips
that stop at the same stops in the same order). Each stop is joined to the
nearest walkable street, and two walking tables are computed once: transfers
between nearby stops (up to 1 km) and walking distances from every stop (up
to 2 km), used to reach destinations.

Each step has fixed rules down to details that only matter on ties: the
order in which ways, feeds and stops are read, which of two equal paths is
kept, and how lengths and speeds are rounded. The same inputs therefore give
the same network, and the same results, whatever the number of threads.

## Street routing

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Street routing: link each point to the nearest street open to the mode; search directed edges from the origin up to the time limit; reach each destination through either end of its edge. Edge costs by mode for walking, cycling and driving."}
fig("street-routing.svg")
```

## Public transport

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Transit travel-time matrix: walk from the origin to stops and destinations; RAPTOR over every departure minute, latest first, with Monte Carlo draws for frequency-based trips; walk from stops to each destination; percentiles over the iterations."}
fig("transit-matrix.svg")
```

The search over public transport is RAPTOR (*Round-bAsed Public Transit
Optimized Router*): round *k* finds the earliest arrival at every stop with
*k* vehicles, so `max_rides` is simply the number of rounds. Running it for
each minute of the window from the last minute back to the first lets each
minute start from the results of the later one ("range RAPTOR"), which is
much cheaper than independent searches.

Frequency-based trips have no fixed departure times. For them every minute is
repeated `draws_per_minute` times with random offsets, drawn from a Mersenne
Twister seeded from `seed` and the origin's coordinates, so the same `seed`
gives the same numbers on every run and with any number of threads.

## Accessibility

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Accessibility: the sum over destinations of opportunities times a decay weight of the travel time, with the five decay functions drawn for a 30 minute cutoff."}
fig("accessibility.svg")
```

## Expanded and arrival matrices

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Expanded matrix: one row per departure minute and draw, with the trip breakdown. Arrival matrix: the latest departure that arrives in time."}
fig("expanded-arrival.svg")
```

For these, the search also keeps, for every stop and iteration, the path that
led there (which vehicles, boarded where and when), so each trip can be
broken down into access, waiting, riding, transfers and egress.

How the results are checked against r5r's is described in
[Coming from r5r](coming-from-r5r.html#parity).

## Credits

The algorithms and their fine print are ported from Conveyal's
[R5](https://github.com/conveyal/r5) 7.6 (MIT licence, © Conveyal), including
RAPTOR as implemented in R5's `FastRaptorWorker`; the decay functions'
exponential reproduces Apache Commons Math 3's `FastMath.exp` (Apache-2.0).
r5r, by Ipea, defined the interface this package follows and supplies the
reference results.
